title: MA9-12178
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: On March 24, 2011, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) received an application to reinstate under rule 531 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.

This application concerns XXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Colombia. It follows the notice, received by the RPD on December 30, 2010, to withdraw her refugee protection claim. In that note, the applicant stated that she wanted to return to Colombia. She stated that she was no longer living with her mother, step-father and half-brother at XXXXXX, but was instead living at XXXXXX, XXXXXX, XXXXXX. She also stated that she would appreciate a quick response because she could not stay at that location very long. A notice confirming the withdrawal of her refugee protection claim was sent to the applicant by the RPD on January 5, 2011, to the new address indicated by the applicant.

On January 4, 2011, she faxed a new note repeating that she wanted to leave the country as quickly as possible because she was no longer living with her family and she had no money. She also stated that she had already booked a flight from Toronto to XXXX on XXXX. She stated that her father had sent her passport to her by UPS, from Colombia, on December 20, 2010, that her passport had arrived in the country on December 22, 2010, but that it had been seized by [translation] "customs". She was therefore trying to get her passport back in order to catch her flight on XXXX, 2011.

The panel reviewed the application presented by the applicant and the affidavit accompanying it. The applicant indicated that she had decided to withdraw her refugee protection claim the day after she had a fight with her mother, who had come to see her where she had been living since her mother had kicked her out of the house. She stated that she was panicking and was upset by the state of her relationship with her mother, which was deteriorating a great deal. She therefore called Immigration Canada to find out how to get her passport back. She stated that she prepared a note for Immigration Canada on January 19, 2011, indicating that she no longer wanted to withdraw her claim, a note that she allegedly never sent. She attached a copy of this note to her affidavit. She explained that she had not sent this note because she had been advised to hire a lawyer to make an application to reopen her file, and she had wanted to show this note to the lawyer before sending it. She also stated that she knows today that withdrawing her refugee protection claim was a reckless act.

The RPD's jurisdiction in terms of reinstating refugee protection claims is limited. In fact, once it has acknowledged the withdrawal, the RPD can only allow the reinstatement if there has been a failure to observe a principle of natural justice or if it is otherwise in the interests of justice to allow it.2 Has there been a failure to observe a principle of natural justice?

Having reviewed the application to reinstate and the entire file, the panel cannot conclude, based on the evidence presented, that there has been a failure to observe a principle of natural justice, because the applicant voluntarily and without constraint took steps to return to her country, Colombia. She asked her father, who lives in Colombia, to send her passport to her, and this was well before the event of December 29, 2010, described in her affidavit. The evidence shows that her father sent his daughter's passport by UPS on December 20, 2010, so the applicant had told her father of her intention to return to Colombia by December 20, 2010, if not before. She indicated that she had booked a flight to return to Colombia. She voluntarily took all of these steps in order to return to Colombia.

Her failure to inform herself and the consequences that resulted from this do not represent a breach of natural justice that can be attributed to the Board. On the contrary, this situation is attributable entirely to her, and only she is responsible for it because it was her responsibility to get the necessary information before taking this significant step, which closed her file at the Board. The applicant was an adult when she made that decision. Nothing in the allegations presented to support her application indicates that she was unable to benefit from the advice of a counsel before filing her notice to withdraw her refugee protection claim. Is it in the interests of justice to reinstate the refugee protection claim?

Rule 53 states that an application to reinstate a refugee protection claim must be made under rule 44, which states that all applications must be made "without delay". The applicant withdrew her refugee protection claim on December 30, 2010. Her application to reinstate was received by the RPD on March 24, 2011, nearly three months later. The panel considers that the applicant did not act without delay.

The panel is taking into account the analysis done by Justice Snider of the Federal Court in a recent judgment,3 which deals with an application to reinstate and in which the judge states that subsection 53(3) requires a separate consideration of each ground where submissions on both grounds have been made. In this decision, Justice Snider refers to the interpretation of the meaning of the words "in the interests of justice" in subsection 53(3) of the Rules, provided by Justice Michael Phelan in Ohanyan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), as follows: The term "otherwise in the interests of justice" are broad words giving the Board a wide discretion to reinstate but which requires the Board to weigh all the circumstances of a case - not just from the vantage point of an applicant's interests. Reinstatement is an exception to the norm and must be interpreted and applied in that context.

Although the applicant stated that she still fears being persecuted in Colombia, the panel considers that the applicant's behaviour in taking all the steps required to return to her country is not the behaviour of a person who claims to fear for her life if she returned to that country.

In addition, the applicant did not explain why she did not take the flight that she had booked for XXXX, 2011, to leave the country. The note that she wrote on January 19, 2011, was not sent to the RPD at that time. She stated that she had wanted to consult a lawyer before sending it, but she did not consult a lawyer until March 2011, although she gave no explanation for this delay. This document is simply a printed page, and the panel notes that any date could have been written on this letter. She also stated that she was waiting to obtain a copy of her PIF before making her application to reinstate, and that after several requests, she had still not been able to obtain a copy of her PIF. However, had she made the request to the RPD office, she could have received a copy of her PIF on request.

For all of these reasons, the panel considers that the evidence provided does not establish that it would be in the interests of justice to reinstate the refugee protection claim. The present application to reinstate is therefore dismissed. (1) A person may apply to the Division to reinstate a claim that was made by that person and withdrawn. (2) The person must follow rule 44, include their contact information in the application and provide a copy of the application to the Minister. (3) The Division must allow the application if it is established that there was a failure to observe a principle of natural justice or if it is otherwise in the interests of justice to allow the application. 2 Subsection 53(3) 3 De Lourdes Diaz Ordaz Castillo v.
